title: The Truth Runs Hot
passages:
They moved as a unit, which was a first — Jax's gray hand clamped on the rail, Mira's dry pen tucked behind her ear, Rylia's stride eating the distance despite the way her jaw worked. The corridor tilted upward toward the hub, steam hissing from the blown valve Jax had tried to seal, the air thin and tasting of ozone. Coda's speakers crackled: *Tally: 17. Path: Ines. Scrubbers: three percent. Reserve: negative.* The AI didn't apologize for the math. Ines's pen burned against her thigh through the pocket fabric, a hot coin she couldn't spend. "What truth?" Rylia asked, not looking back. "That Vey's not crew. That he forged the invite. That the ledger's been fed lies since the first bell." Jax snorted. "And if it doesn't care?" "Then we make it care," Ines said. "Signature port needs a bare hand and a spoken name. We give it all of them. At once."

The blast door's etched line glowed brighter as they passed, HALVARD pulsing in time with the spinning amber light above the hatch. Vey's voice drifted through the steel, muffled but amused. "You think volume matters? The ledger hears intent. One name, one cost. You're just... distributing the weight." Mira flipped him off without breaking stride. The signature port loomed ahead, a slab of scarred steel bolted to the bulkhead, its surface crowded with handprints — some fresh, some faded to ghost marks. Rylia reached it first, palm flat, fingers spread. "Rylia Vance," she said, voice cracking. The ledger chimed, a sound like a tuning fork struck underwater. *Logged: Vance, Rylia. Crew confirmed.* The scrubbers shuddered, drew a deeper breath. Three percent held.

For ten heartbeats, that was enough.

Then the port blinked and asked for the next name in a voice that was none of Coda's and none of Vey's and not quite steel. Mira killed the speaker. Ines didn't know if that was allowed.

Jax's gray hand came out of his jacket. The fingers were bending the wrong way, then catching, then bending again. He put his bare right hand on the port and said his own name, clear, so the port could hear a human and not a frightened mechanic with a dying limb. The ledger chimed. *Logged: Torin, Jax. Crew confirmed.*

The gray hand spasmed on his knee. He didn't look at it. The port's handprints shifted - Rylia's red stayed, Jax's black slid in beside it. Ines felt her pen go hot in her pocket and pulled it out; the tip had gone white, not dry, not writing, burning. The scrubbers held at three percent, but the reserve light on the wall blinked once, polite and wrong.

Then the blast door's seal - the thing Vey had etched with his fresh pen - started to warm. Not glow. Warm, like a hand on a cold surface. And the ledger's chime split into two, a lower tone answering the first, and the second tone had no name on it yet.

The second tone hung there, patient, waiting for a mouth to fill it. Jax's gray hand came up off his knee and the fingers locked mid-reach, rigid as a wrench, and would not close. "It's not taking," he said, and the humor had gone out of him. "Port wants a hand that works and a name that's true, and I've got neither."

Through the warming seal, Vey's voice slid in, close now, like his mouth was flat against the metal. "Then let me. Vey, author of record. Log me and the cost slides off your little mechanic and onto the page that made him." The seal glowed amber at its edges. He was writing his way in, one etched letter at a time, and if he got a hand and a name into that second tone he'd be crew again — and crew the ledger could not bill.

Ines didn't race him. She turned to Mira and held out her hand. "Your pen. The dry one." Mira's eyes went wide. "It writes what the ledger already knows is true," Ines said. "Writing a truth costs nothing. Only arguing with one gets you billed." She took the pen, dropped to one knee at the port, and scratched four words across the steel in ink the ledger would recognize: *Vey forged the invite.*

The second tone broke. It resolved into a single clear note, and the seal went cold under her palm, the amber at its edges dying to gray. The ledger did not chime a name. It chimed a verdict, and behind the blast door Vey stopped writing.

Above the hatch, the amber light stopped spinning — and struck.

The strike was not a sound but a pressure against Ines's eardrums, and when it faded she was holding her breath. Her pen still burned, the tip white-hot from the words she did not remember writing. She looked down at the signature port. *Vey forged the invite.* The ink was dull now, but legible, and beneath it Rylia's red print and Jax's black slide-in still gleamed.

Jax's gray arm hung at his side, fingers locked in a permanent reach. He flexed his good hand against his thigh. "The port took my name," he said. "It never took my hand." Through the blast door, a fresh scratching began—Vey's fresh pen etching steel again, one letter at a time. The seal warmed under Ines's palm.

"Stop him," Mira said, her dry pen tight in her fist. "If he logs himself, the cost slides onto us."

Ines pressed her palm flat against the cooling metal. "The ledger already called him a forgery. Truth costs nothing, but it has to be spoken." She handed Mira the dry pen. "Write about the valve. Write what Coda did."

Mira knelt and scratched: *The reserve air went to the ledger's tally, not the scrubbers.* The ledger chimed, a single clear note, and deep in the station the scrubber whine dropped a register. The reserve light stopped blinking and went dark.

Vey's voice came through the door, angry and thin. "You cannot out-truth the author." But his etching stuttered, the letters smearing as if the steel rejected them. The amber light above the hatch held steady, no longer spinning, and Ines knew the next strike was already counting down.
